title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast… but Risky ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First “rush” toward the goal using only the heuristic distance, creating a path that looks smart—until it gets trapped by misleading routes. Then compare the behavior to Greedy vs A* thinking: what changes when the algorithm also accounts for path cost?
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — why Greedy rushes toward destinations and when it fails ⚡

In this Lisbon (Alfama) visualization, Greedy Best-First uses a heuristic pathfinding estimate (think “straight-line distance” to the target) to always expand the node that *looks* closest.

✅ What you’ll see:
• The frontier picks the smallest h(n) first (goal-chasing behavior)
• It can produce a quick-looking route early
• But it may ignore the real cost so it can detour, loop, or dead-end when the heuristic lies

🔧 Technical breakdown (simple):
Greedy priority = h(n)
A* priority = g(n) + h(n) (adds actual path cost so it’s less easily fooled)

Takeaway: Heuristic pathfinding alone can be greedy—fast decisions, potentially wrong direction.

Debate: In your own code—would you rather optimize for *speed-to-looks-right* or *guaranteed optimal-ish* results? 👇
